questions.commandDemand: Give the cause and the process. Do not stop at what you saw; say what caused it and name the process.
questions.stimulus: A puddle on the road disappears after a hot afternoon.
questions.stem: Explain why the puddle disappeared.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the water evaporated
the water gained heat energy from the sun
it changed into water vapour

chain.text: Water in the puddle gained heat energy from the sun.
The water evaporated, changing from the liquid state to water vapour.
The water vapour escaped into the air, so the puddle disappeared.

questions.modelAnswer: Water in the puddle gained heat energy from the sun. This caused the water to evaporate, changing from the liquid state into water vapour. The water vapour escaped into the surrounding air, so the puddle disappeared.
markPoints: Water gained heat energy from the sun
Water evaporated / changed from liquid to water vapour
questions.whyMarksLost: Most answers say 'the water dried up in the sun'. That names the observation, not the process. The marks are for naming evaporation and for saying the water gained heat energy.

questions.commandDemand: Give the cause and the process behind the observation.
questions.stimulus: Water droplets form on the outside of a glass of iced water left on a table.
questions.stem: Explain how the water droplets formed on the outside of the glass.

fuzzyTraps.vague: water came out of the glass
fuzzyTraps.precise: water vapour in the air condensed on the glass
the water vapour lost heat energy to the cold glass

chain.text: Water vapour in the surrounding air touches the cold surface of the glass.
The water vapour loses heat energy to the colder glass and condenses.
It changes into liquid water, forming droplets on the outside of the glass.

questions.modelAnswer: Water vapour in the surrounding air came into contact with the cold surface of the glass. The water vapour lost heat energy to the colder glass and condensed, changing from the gaseous state into liquid water. This formed droplets on the outside of the glass.
markPoints: Water vapour in the air loses heat to the cold glass
Water vapour condenses / changes from gas to liquid
questions.whyMarksLost: A very common wrong answer is that the water leaked through the glass. The examiner wants the source named as water vapour in the air, and the process named as condensation.

questions.commandDemand: State what will happen, then give the reason. A prediction without a reason scores half.
questions.stimulus: Two identical dishes hold 50 ml of water each. Dish A is left in a shaded corner. Dish B is left beside a sunny window. Both are checked after four hours.
questions.stem: Predict which dish will contain less water after four hours, and explain your answer.

fuzzyTraps.vague: B loses more because it is hotter
fuzzyTraps.precise: B receives more heat energy, so the rate of evaporation is higher

chain.text: Dish B will contain less water.
Dish B receives more heat energy from the sunlight.
More heat energy increases the rate of evaporation.

questions.modelAnswer: Dish B will contain less water. Dish B receives more heat energy from the sunlight than Dish A. The greater the heat energy gained, the higher the rate of evaporation, so more water in Dish B evaporates in the same four hours.
markPoints: Dish B contains less water
Dish B gains more heat energy, so its rate of evaporation is higher
questions.whyMarksLost: Naming the dish alone earns one mark at most. The second mark needs the words rate of evaporation linked to heat energy.

questions.commandDemand: State what happens, in order. No reasons needed, but the sequence must be complete and in the right order.
questions.stem: Describe how water from the sea ends up falling as rain.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the water evaporates and the water vapour rises

fuzzyTraps.vague: clouds get heavy and drop water
fuzzyTraps.precise: the water droplets combine until they are heavy enough to fall as rain

chain.text: Water at the sea surface gains heat energy from the sun and evaporates into water vapour.
The water vapour rises, cools, loses heat energy and condenses into tiny water droplets, forming clouds.
The droplets combine until they are heavy enough to fall as rain.

questions.modelAnswer: Water at the surface of the sea gains heat energy from the sun and evaporates, changing into water vapour. The water vapour rises and cools. As it loses heat energy it condenses into tiny water droplets, which collect to form clouds. The droplets combine until they become heavy enough to fall to the ground as rain.
markPoints: Evaporation of sea water into water vapour using heat from the sun
Water vapour rises, cools and condenses into droplets forming clouds
Droplets combine and become heavy enough to fall as rain
questions.whyMarksLost: Three marks means three distinct stages. Answers that jump from the sea straight to rain lose the condensation mark, which is the one the examiner most wants to see.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a sensible method or reason. There may be more than one right answer, but it must be practical and it must work.
questions.stimulus: A family hangs wet laundry indoors on a rainy day. The clothes take a very long time to dry.
questions.stem: Suggest two things the family could do to make the clothes dry faster indoors, and explain why each would work.

fuzzyTraps.vague: put a fan so it blows the water away
fuzzyTraps.precise: moving air removes water vapour from around the clothes, increasing the rate of evaporation

chain.text: Switch on a fan to blow air over the clothes.
Moving air carries away water vapour, increasing the rate of evaporation.
Spread the clothes out rather than bunching them.
A larger exposed surface area increases the rate of evaporation.

questions.modelAnswer: The family could switch on a fan so that air moves over the clothes. Moving air carries away the water vapour near the wet cloth, which increases the rate of evaporation. They could also spread the clothes out instead of bunching them together. This increases the exposed surface area of the wet cloth, which also increases the rate of evaporation.
markPoints: One workable suggestion with the reason linked to rate of evaporation
A second workable suggestion with its reason linked to rate of evaporation
questions.whyMarksLost: Suggest questions still need reasons. Listing two ideas with no explanation scores half. Every reason should end at the phrase rate of evaporation.

questions.commandDemand: Read the evidence given and state the conclusion it supports. Quote the evidence, then state what it shows.
questions.stimulus:
Four identical wet cloths were left in different places. The time taken for each to dry completely was recorded.

Cloth W, shaded and still air: 300 minutes
Cloth X, shaded and windy: 180 minutes
Cloth Y, sunny and still air: 140 minutes
Cloth Z, sunny and windy: 80 minutes
questions.stem: What can you infer about the conditions that affect how quickly water evaporates?

fuzzyTraps.precise: both greater heat energy and moving air increase the rate of evaporation

chain.text: Comparing W with Y, the sunny cloth dried faster in the same still air.
Comparing W with X, the windy cloth dried faster in the same shade.
Both heat energy and moving air increase the rate of evaporation.

questions.modelAnswer: Comparing Cloth W with Cloth Y, where only the sunlight differed, the cloth in the sun dried faster. This shows that more heat energy increases the rate of evaporation. Comparing Cloth W with Cloth X, where only the air movement differed, the windy cloth dried faster. This shows that moving air also increases the rate of evaporation.
markPoints: More heat energy increases the rate of evaporation, supported by a valid comparison
Moving air increases the rate of evaporation, supported by a valid comparison
questions.whyMarksLost: Inference answers must name the two cloths being compared. Saying 'Z was fastest so sun and wind help' does not show which factor caused what, because two things changed at once.

questions.commandDemand: Give the mechanism. The answer must connect the observation to the water cycle.
questions.stimulus: A gardener covers a potted plant with a clear plastic bag. After a day, droplets of water are seen on the inside of the bag.
questions.stem: Explain how the water droplets got onto the inside of the plastic bag.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the plant loses water vapour through transpiration

fuzzyTraps.vague: the water stuck to the bag
fuzzyTraps.precise: the water vapour condensed on the cooler surface of the bag

chain.text: The plant loses water as water vapour through its leaves by transpiration.
The water vapour is trapped by the bag and loses heat energy at the cooler bag surface.
It condenses into liquid water droplets on the inside of the bag.

questions.modelAnswer: The plant lost water as water vapour through its leaves by transpiration. The water vapour was trapped inside the plastic bag. When it came into contact with the cooler surface of the bag, it lost heat energy and condensed, changing into liquid water droplets on the inside of the bag.
markPoints: Water vapour released by the plant through transpiration
Water vapour condenses on the cooler surface of the bag
questions.whyMarksLost: The word transpiration is the mark. 'The plant gave out water' describes it but does not name it, and at AL1 the examiner expects the term.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the properties of the state of matter.
questions.stimulus: A helium balloon is squeezed. Its shape changes, but the amount of gas inside stays the same.
questions.stem: Explain why the gas inside the balloon can change shape when squeezed.

fuzzyTraps.precise: a gas has no definite shape
a gas takes the shape of its container

chain.text: A gas has no definite shape.
It takes the shape of whatever container holds it.
When the balloon is squeezed the gas fills the new shape of the balloon.

questions.modelAnswer: A gas has no definite shape. It takes the shape of the container it is in. When the balloon is squeezed, the gas inside fills the new shape of the balloon, so its shape changes even though the amount of gas stays the same.
markPoints: A gas has no definite shape
A gas takes the shape of its container
questions.whyMarksLost: Answers about the balloon being stretchy describe the rubber, not the gas. The question asks about the gas, so the answer must use the properties of a gas.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using a property that distinguishes the two states.
questions.stimulus: Water is poured from a tall narrow jug into a wide flat dish. A wooden block is moved from the jug to the dish.
questions.stem: Explain why the water changes shape but the wooden block does not.

fuzzyTraps.precise: a liquid has no definite shape
a solid has a definite shape

chain.text: Water is a liquid, and a liquid has no definite shape.
The block is a solid, and a solid has a definite shape.
The liquid takes the shape of its container; the solid keeps its own shape.

questions.modelAnswer: Water is a liquid. A liquid has no definite shape and takes the shape of the container it is poured into, so it spreads out in the wide dish. The wooden block is a solid. A solid has a definite shape of its own, so it does not change shape when moved into the dish.
markPoints: A liquid has no definite shape and takes the shape of its container
A solid has a definite shape of its own
questions.whyMarksLost: Both halves are needed. Explaining only the water leaves the second mark unclaimed, because the question compares two things.

questions.commandDemand: State what is observed at each stage. The order matters.
questions.stimulus: A block of ice is taken from the freezer, left on a table until it melts, then heated in a pan until it boils away.
questions.stem: Describe the changes of state that the water goes through, and name each change.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the ice melts, changing from the solid state to the liquid state
the water boils, changing from the liquid state to the gaseous state

chain.text: The ice gains heat energy and melts from solid to liquid.
The liquid water continues to gain heat energy.
At its boiling point the water boils, changing from liquid to water vapour.

questions.modelAnswer: The ice gains heat energy from the surroundings and melts, changing from the solid state into the liquid state. The liquid water continues to gain heat energy in the pan. When it reaches its boiling point it boils, changing from the liquid state into the gaseous state as water vapour.
markPoints: Melting: solid to liquid, gaining heat energy
Water gains heat energy until it reaches its boiling point
Boiling: liquid to gas
questions.whyMarksLost: Naming the states without naming the changes, or the reverse, costs marks. The examiner wants both the name of the process and the states it moves between.

questions.commandDemand: Use the data to reach a conclusion. Point at the evidence in the table.
questions.stimulus:
A student measured the volume and the shape of three substances after moving each into differently shaped containers.

Substance P: shape changed, volume stayed the same
Substance Q: shape stayed the same, volume stayed the same
Substance R: shape changed, volume changed to fill the container
questions.stem: Infer the state of matter of substances P, Q and R. Give a reason for each.

fuzzyTraps.vague: R is a gas because it spreads
fuzzyTraps.precise: R is a gas because it has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume

chain.text: No definite shape but a definite volume, so P is a liquid.
Definite shape and definite volume, so Q is a solid.
Neither definite shape nor definite volume, so R is a gas.

questions.modelAnswer: P is a liquid, because it has no definite shape but has a definite volume. Q is a solid, because it has both a definite shape and a definite volume. R is a gas, because it has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume and fills its container completely.
markPoints: All three states correctly identified
Each reason given using definite shape and definite volume
questions.whyMarksLost: Naming the three states with no reasons scores one mark only. The reason must use the words definite shape and definite volume, because those are the properties the table is testing.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason. The answer must refer to mass and to the fact that matter is conserved.
questions.stimulus: A sealed bottle containing ice is weighed. The ice is left to melt completely, and the sealed bottle is weighed again.
questions.stem: Explain why the mass of the sealed bottle stays the same after the ice melts.

fuzzyTraps.precise: no matter entered or left the sealed bottle

fuzzyTraps.vague: it is still the same water
fuzzyTraps.precise: melting is a change of state, so the amount of matter is unchanged

chain.text: The bottle is sealed, so no matter can enter or leave.
Melting is only a change of state, from solid to liquid.
The amount of matter, and therefore the mass, is unchanged.

questions.modelAnswer: The bottle is sealed, so no matter can enter or leave it. Melting is only a change of state from the solid state to the liquid state; it does not create or destroy matter. Since the amount of matter inside the bottle is unchanged, the mass stays the same.
markPoints: No matter enters or leaves the sealed bottle
A change of state does not change the amount of matter, so mass is unchanged
questions.whyMarksLost: 'It is the same water' is the idea but not the language. The mark is for saying that a change of state does not change the amount of matter.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a workable method and say why it works.
questions.stimulus: A student is given a sealed box and told it contains one substance. She is not allowed to open it, but she may tilt it and weigh it.
questions.stem: Suggest how the student could find out whether the substance inside is a solid or a liquid.

fuzzyTraps.precise: tilt it and observe whether the contents flow to take the new shape

chain.text: Tilt the box slowly and feel or listen for the contents moving.
A liquid has no definite shape and will flow to fill the lower part of the box.
A solid keeps its definite shape and will not flow.

questions.modelAnswer: The student could tilt the box slowly and observe whether the contents shift to fill the lower part. A liquid has no definite shape and will flow to take the shape of the container as it is tilted. A solid has a definite shape and will not flow, so if the contents do not shift the substance is a solid.
markPoints: A workable test based on tilting the box
Reason given using definite shape, with what each result would mean
questions.whyMarksLost: A method without a prediction of what each outcome means is incomplete. Say what a liquid would do and what a solid would do.

questions.commandDemand: Give both similarities and differences, and make each point about both things.
questions.stem: Compare the properties of a liquid and a gas.

fuzzyTraps.precise: a gas has no definite volume, while a liquid has a definite volume

chain.text: Both a liquid and a gas have no definite shape and take the shape of their container.
A liquid has a definite volume; a gas does not.
A gas fills its container completely, while a liquid only fills part of it.

questions.modelAnswer: Both a liquid and a gas have no definite shape, and both take the shape of the container they are in. However, a liquid has a definite volume while a gas has no definite volume. This means a gas will spread out and fill its container completely, whereas a liquid will only occupy the lower part of the container.
markPoints: Similarity: neither has a definite shape; both take the shape of the container
Difference: a liquid has a definite volume, a gas does not
Consequence: a gas fills the container completely, a liquid does not
questions.whyMarksLost: Compare means both. Answers that only list differences drop the similarity mark. Also, each sentence should mention both the liquid and the gas, not one at a time.

questions.commandDemand: Give a similarity and a difference, and refer to both animals in each point.
questions.stem: Compare the life cycle of a butterfly with the life cycle of a grasshopper.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the butterfly undergoes complete metamorphosis, with a pupa stage
the nymph resembles the adult but is smaller and lacks wings

chain.text: Both begin life as an egg and both undergo metamorphosis.
The butterfly has four stages including a pupa; the grasshopper has three and no pupa.
The grasshopper nymph resembles the adult, while the butterfly larva does not.

questions.modelAnswer: Both the butterfly and the grasshopper begin life as an egg and both undergo metamorphosis. However, the butterfly undergoes complete metamorphosis with four stages, egg, larva, pupa and adult, while the grasshopper undergoes incomplete metamorphosis with three stages, egg, nymph and adult. The grasshopper nymph resembles the adult but is smaller and has no wings, whereas the butterfly larva looks completely different from the adult.
markPoints: Similarity: both start as an egg and undergo metamorphosis
Difference: complete metamorphosis with a pupa stage versus incomplete metamorphosis with a nymph stage
questions.whyMarksLost: The terms complete metamorphosis and incomplete metamorphosis are what the examiner is looking for. Describing the stages without naming the two types leaves marks behind.

questions.commandDemand: Give the advantage and say why it is an advantage for survival.
questions.stimulus: A butterfly larva feeds on leaves. The adult butterfly feeds on nectar from flowers.
questions.stem: Explain how this difference in diet is an advantage to the butterfly.

fuzzyTraps.vague: they do not fight over food
fuzzyTraps.precise: they do not compete with each other for the same food source

chain.text: The larva and the adult eat different foods.
They therefore do not compete for the same food source.
More of both stages can obtain enough food and survive.

questions.modelAnswer: The larva and the adult butterfly feed on different food sources. This means they do not compete with each other for the same food. More individuals at both stages are therefore able to obtain enough food, which increases their chance of survival.
markPoints: The larva and adult do not compete for the same food source
This increases the chance of survival of both stages
questions.whyMarksLost: The word competition is the key term. Answers that say 'there is more food for everyone' are close but do not name the idea the mark scheme is built around.

questions.commandDemand: Use the data to identify the animal type or stage, and justify from the evidence.
questions.stimulus:
A scientist recorded the stages of four animals.

Animal A: egg, larva, pupa, adult
Animal B: egg, nymph, adult
Animal C: egg, young, adult, with the young hatching in water and later growing legs
Animal D: young born alive, adult
questions.stem: Infer which animal is most likely to be a frog, and give a reason.

fuzzyTraps.precise: C hatches in water as a tadpole and later develops legs, matching a frog's life cycle

chain.text: Animal C hatches from an egg in water and later grows legs.
A frog hatches as a tadpole in water and develops legs as it matures.
Animal C is most likely the frog.

questions.modelAnswer: Animal C is most likely the frog. A frog lays eggs in water, and the young hatch as tadpoles which live in water. As the tadpole matures it develops legs and becomes an adult frog, which matches the stages recorded for Animal C.
markPoints: Animal C identified
Reason linked to hatching in water and later developing legs, as a tadpole does
questions.whyMarksLost: Choosing the right animal without quoting the evidence from the table earns one mark. Infer questions always want the evidence stated.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and give the reason based on the life cycle.
questions.stimulus: A farmer sprays a chemical on his crops that kills only the larvae of a particular moth. The adult moths are unharmed.
questions.stem: Predict what will happen to the number of adult moths over the next few months, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the number of adult moths will decrease

fuzzyTraps.vague: the babies die so no more come
fuzzyTraps.precise: the larvae cannot develop into adults, so fewer adults are produced

chain.text: The number of adult moths will decrease.
The larvae are killed before they can complete the life cycle.
Fewer larvae survive to develop into pupae and then into adults.

questions.modelAnswer: The number of adult moths will decrease. The chemical kills the larvae, so fewer larvae survive to develop into pupae and then into adult moths. Since the adult stage can only be reached by passing through the larval stage, fewer adults will be produced over the next few months.
markPoints: The number of adult moths decreases
Reason: larvae are killed before they can develop into adults, breaking the life cycle
questions.whyMarksLost: The reasoning mark needs the idea that every adult must pass through the larval stage. Without that link the answer is a guess rather than a prediction.

questions.commandDemand: State the stages in order and name each one.
questions.stem: Describe the life cycle of a mosquito.

fuzzyTraps.vague: it starts as a baby in water
fuzzyTraps.precise: the egg hatches into a larva which lives in water

chain.text: The adult lays eggs in stagnant water.
The eggs hatch into larvae, which live in the water.
Each larva develops into a pupa, then emerges as an adult mosquito.

questions.modelAnswer: The adult mosquito lays its eggs in stagnant water. The eggs hatch into larvae, which live in the water. Each larva then develops into a pupa, and the adult mosquito finally emerges from the pupa and flies away. This is complete metamorphosis, with four stages.
markPoints: All four stages named in the correct order: egg, larva, pupa, adult
Identified as complete metamorphosis, or the aquatic stages noted
questions.whyMarksLost: Missing the pupa stage is the most common error and costs the mark, because the pupa is what makes this complete metamorphosis.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a practical action and explain how it breaks the life cycle.
questions.stimulus: A neighbourhood has a problem with mosquitoes. Residents are asked to help reduce the mosquito population.
questions.stem: Suggest one action residents could take, and explain how it would reduce the number of mosquitoes.

fuzzyTraps.precise: remove stagnant water so the larvae cannot develop

chain.text: Remove or empty any containers holding stagnant water.
Mosquitoes lay eggs in stagnant water and the larvae need water to develop.
Without stagnant water the life cycle is broken and fewer adults emerge.

questions.modelAnswer: Residents could empty any containers holding stagnant water, such as flower pot trays. Mosquitoes lay their eggs in stagnant water, and the larvae and pupae need water to develop. Without stagnant water the eggs cannot hatch and develop, so the life cycle is broken and fewer adult mosquitoes are produced.
markPoints: Practical action: remove or empty stagnant water
Explanation linked to the larval stage needing water, breaking the life cycle
questions.whyMarksLost: Suggesting the action without explaining which stage it attacks scores one mark. Name the stage that depends on the water.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the idea of a stage that does not feed or move.
questions.stimulus: A student watching a caterpillar notices it stops eating and becomes still inside a hard case for two weeks. It then emerges as a butterfly.
questions.stem: Explain what is happening inside the hard case during those two weeks.

fuzzyTraps.precise: it is in the pupa stage, undergoing metamorphosis
its body structures are reorganised into those of the adult

chain.text: The hard case is the pupa stage of the life cycle.
Inside the pupa the larva's body undergoes metamorphosis.
Its body structures develop into those of the adult butterfly.

questions.modelAnswer: The hard case is the pupa stage of the butterfly's life cycle. Inside the pupa, the larva undergoes metamorphosis. Its body structures are broken down and reorganised into those of the adult, such as wings and legs. When this development is complete, the adult butterfly emerges.
markPoints: The stage is named as the pupa
Metamorphosis occurs, with body structures developing into those of the adult
questions.whyMarksLost: 'It is resting' or 'it is sleeping' gets no marks. The pupa is not inactive; the mark is for saying that development is taking place.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason. Link the structure to the method of dispersal.
questions.stimulus: A seed has a light, papery wing attached to one side.
questions.stem: Explain how this seed is dispersed.

fuzzyTraps.precise: it is carried away by the wind
the wing increases the surface area, so the wind can carry it further

chain.text: The seed has a light, papery wing.
The wing increases the surface area while the seed stays light.
The wind can carry the seed further from the parent plant.

questions.modelAnswer: The seed is dispersed by wind. The light, papery wing increases the surface area of the seed while keeping it light. This allows the seed to be carried by the wind and blown further away from the parent plant.
markPoints: Dispersed by wind
The wing increases surface area and the seed is light, so it is carried further
questions.whyMarksLost: Saying 'by wind' alone is one mark. The second mark is for linking the structure, the wing, to the property that makes wind dispersal work.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason. This is about competition, so the word must appear.
questions.stem: Explain why it is an advantage for a plant if its seeds are dispersed far away from the parent plant.

fuzzyTraps.precise: they do not compete with the parent plant for space
there is less competition for water and mineral salts

chain.text: The seeds land away from the parent plant.
They do not compete with the parent or with each other for resources.
More seedlings obtain enough sunlight, water and mineral salts to grow.

questions.modelAnswer: If the seeds land far from the parent plant, the seedlings do not have to compete with the parent plant or with one another for sunlight, water, mineral salts and space. With less competition, more of the seedlings can obtain the resources they need and grow successfully.
markPoints: Less competition with the parent plant and with other seedlings
Named resources: sunlight, water, mineral salts or space
questions.whyMarksLost: The resources must be named. 'They get more nutrients' is too vague; the mark scheme wants sunlight, water and mineral salts.

questions.commandDemand: Read the results and state which factor is needed, quoting the comparison.
questions.stimulus:
Four sets of identical seeds were placed in different conditions for one week.

Set 1, moist cotton wool, warm, in light: germinated
Set 2, dry cotton wool, warm, in light: did not germinate
Set 3, moist cotton wool, warm, in darkness: germinated
Set 4, moist cotton wool, in a fridge, in light: did not germinate
questions.stem: What can you infer about the conditions needed for germination?

fuzzyTraps.precise: seeds need water and warmth, but not light

chain.text: Set 1 germinated and Set 2 did not; only water differed, so water is needed.
Set 1 germinated and Set 4 did not; only warmth differed, so warmth is needed.
Set 3 germinated in darkness, so light is not needed.

questions.modelAnswer: Seeds need water and warmth for germination, but they do not need light. Comparing Set 1 with Set 2, where only the water differed, only the moist set germinated, so water is needed. Comparing Set 1 with Set 4, where only the temperature differed, only the warm set germinated, so warmth is needed. Set 3 germinated in darkness, which shows that light is not needed.
markPoints: Water and warmth are needed, each supported by a valid pair comparison
Light is not needed, supported by Set 3
questions.whyMarksLost: Many students add light to the list because Set 1 had light. Set 3 disproves it. Always look for the set that isolates the factor.

questions.commandDemand: State the stages in order.
questions.stem: Describe the life cycle of a flowering plant, starting from the seed.

fuzzyTraps.precise: the seed germinates

chain.text: The seed germinates and grows into a seedling.
The seedling grows into an adult plant which produces flowers.
The flowers are pollinated and produce fruits with seeds, which are dispersed.

questions.modelAnswer: The seed germinates and grows into a seedling. The seedling grows into an adult plant, which then produces flowers. After pollination and fertilisation, the flowers develop into fruits containing seeds. These seeds are dispersed and can germinate to begin the cycle again.
markPoints: Germination into a seedling, then growth into an adult plant that flowers
Flowers produce seeds which are dispersed and germinate, completing the cycle
questions.whyMarksLost: The word germinates is worth having. 'The seed grows into a plant' skips the named process the examiner is checking for.

questions.commandDemand: State what happens and give the reason from the plant's needs.
questions.stimulus: A gardener sows fifty seeds very close together in a small pot. All of them germinate.
questions.stem: Predict what will happen to the seedlings as they grow, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.precise: they will compete with one another for resources
some seedlings will grow poorly or die

chain.text: Many of the seedlings will grow poorly, and some will die.
They are close together in a small pot with limited resources.
They compete for sunlight, water and mineral salts, so some do not get enough.

questions.modelAnswer: Many of the seedlings will grow poorly and some will die. Because they are sown very close together in a small pot, the seedlings compete with one another for sunlight, water and mineral salts. There are not enough of these resources for all fifty, so the seedlings that cannot obtain enough will not grow well.
markPoints: Some seedlings grow poorly or die
Reason: competition for named limited resources
questions.whyMarksLost: The prediction alone is one mark. The second needs the word competition and at least two named resources.

questions.commandDemand: Link the structure of the fruit to its method of dispersal.
questions.stimulus: A fruit is brightly coloured, sweet and fleshy, and contains hard seeds that are not digested by animals.
questions.stem: Explain how the seeds of this fruit are dispersed.

fuzzyTraps.precise: animals eat the fruit and the seeds pass out in their droppings

chain.text: The fruit is brightly coloured and sweet, which attracts animals.
Animals eat the fruit, and the hard seeds are not digested.
The seeds pass out in the animals' droppings away from the parent plant.

questions.modelAnswer: The seeds are dispersed by animals. The bright colour and sweet, fleshy fruit attract animals to eat it. The hard seeds are not digested, so they pass out of the animal in its droppings at a place away from the parent plant, where they can germinate.
markPoints: Dispersed by animals, attracted by the colour or sweetness
Seeds are not digested and pass out in droppings away from the parent plant
questions.whyMarksLost: The detail that the seeds are not digested is the mark most often missed. It is the reason the seed survives the journey.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a workable design and justify it with the dispersal method.
questions.stimulus: A student is asked to design a model seed that will travel as far as possible when dropped from a height in still air.
questions.stem: Suggest two features the model seed should have, and explain why each helps.

fuzzyTraps.vague: make it float in the air
fuzzyTraps.precise: a large surface area increases air resistance so it falls slowly

chain.text: A large surface area, such as wings or hairs.
This increases air resistance, so the seed falls more slowly and stays airborne longer.
A low mass, so the seed is light.
A lighter seed is more easily carried, so it travels further.

questions.modelAnswer: The model seed should have a large surface area, for example papery wings or fine hairs. This increases the air resistance acting on it, so it falls more slowly and stays in the air longer. It should also be very light. A seed with a small mass is more easily carried by moving air, so it can travel further from where it was released.
markPoints: Large surface area, with the reason linked to air resistance and slower falling
Light or low mass, with the reason linked to being carried further
questions.whyMarksLost: Two features are asked for, so two reasons are needed. Also, air resistance is the precise term; 'the air pushes it up' will not score.

questions.commandDemand: State what happens, naming the parts involved.
questions.stem: Describe what happens during pollination in a flowering plant.

fuzzyTraps.vague: the pollen moves to the flower
fuzzyTraps.precise: pollen grains are transferred from the anther to the stigma

chain.text: Pollen grains are produced in the anther.
The pollen grains are transferred to the stigma.
This transfer is carried out by an agent such as an insect or the wind.

questions.modelAnswer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a flower to the stigma. The pollen grains are carried by an agent of pollination, such as an insect or the wind. Once on the stigma, the pollen grain can grow a pollen tube down the style towards the ovule.
markPoints: Transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma
Carried out by an agent such as insects or wind
questions.whyMarksLost: Anther and stigma must both be named. Saying pollen moves 'from one flower to another' describes cross pollination but misses the parts.

questions.commandDemand: Link each feature to how it helps that method of pollination.
questions.stimulus: Flower P has large, brightly coloured petals and produces a sweet scent and nectar. Flower Q has small, dull, unscented petals and produces large amounts of light pollen.
questions.stem: Explain which flower is pollinated by insects and which by wind.

fuzzyTraps.vague: P is pretty so insects like it
fuzzyTraps.precise: the bright petals, scent and nectar attract insects

fuzzyTraps.vague: Q has lots of pollen so wind blows it
fuzzyTraps.precise: large amounts of light pollen are easily carried by the wind

chain.text: Bright petals, scent and nectar attract insects, so P is insect pollinated.
Dull, unscented flowers do not attract insects.
Large amounts of light pollen are easily carried away by the wind, so Q is wind pollinated.

questions.modelAnswer: Flower P is pollinated by insects. Its large, brightly coloured petals, sweet scent and nectar attract insects, which pick up pollen and carry it to another flower. Flower Q is pollinated by wind. Its small, dull and unscented petals do not attract insects, and it produces large amounts of light pollen that can easily be carried away by moving air.
markPoints: P is insect pollinated, with features linked to attracting insects
Q is wind pollinated, with light or plentiful pollen linked to being carried by air
questions.whyMarksLost: Identifying both flowers with no feature linked to a reason scores one mark. Each identification needs its own justification.

questions.commandDemand: State the outcome and explain using the reproduction process.
questions.stimulus: A farmer grows an orchard of fruit trees inside a large sealed greenhouse. No insects can enter, and there is no wind inside.
questions.stem: Predict what will happen to the number of fruits produced, and explain why.

fuzzyTraps.precise: without an agent of pollination, pollen cannot be transferred to the stigma

chain.text: Very few or no fruits will be produced.
There is no insect or wind to act as an agent of pollination.
Without pollination there is no fertilisation, and fruits develop only after fertilisation.

questions.modelAnswer: Very few or no fruits will be produced. There are no insects and no moving air inside the greenhouse to act as agents of pollination, so pollen grains cannot be transferred from the anther to the stigma. Without pollination, fertilisation cannot take place, and fruits only develop after fertilisation has occurred.
markPoints: Few or no fruits produced
No agent of pollination, so no pollination and therefore no fertilisation
questions.whyMarksLost: The chain has three links: no agent, no pollination, no fertilisation. Skipping fertilisation is the usual reason this drops to one mark.

questions.commandDemand: Offer a practical solution and explain the mechanism by which it works.
questions.stimulus: The same farmer wants his sealed greenhouse to produce fruit without opening it to the outside.
questions.stem: Suggest what the farmer could do, and explain how it would work.

fuzzyTraps.precise: introduce insects into the greenhouse to act as agents of pollination

chain.text: Introduce insects such as bees into the greenhouse, or pollinate the flowers by hand.
This transfers pollen grains from the anther to the stigma.
Pollination allows fertilisation, so fruits can develop.

questions.modelAnswer: The farmer could release insects such as bees into the greenhouse, or transfer the pollen himself using a small brush. Either method transfers pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the flowers. This allows pollination and then fertilisation to take place, so the flowers can develop into fruits.
markPoints: A workable method of transferring pollen, by insects or by hand
Explained as transfer from anther to stigma allowing fertilisation
questions.whyMarksLost: 'Use bees' alone is one mark. The explanation must say what the bees actually do, in the language of anther and stigma.

questions.commandDemand: Give the reason using the function of the flower part named.
questions.stimulus: A student removes all the anthers from a flower bud before it opens, then covers the flower with a bag.
questions.stem: Explain why this flower will not produce any seeds.

fuzzyTraps.vague: there is nothing to make seeds
fuzzyTraps.precise: no pollen grains are produced, so pollination cannot occur

chain.text: The anthers, which produce pollen grains, have been removed.
The bag also prevents pollen from other flowers reaching the stigma.
Without pollination there is no fertilisation, so no seeds form.

questions.modelAnswer: The anthers produce the pollen grains, and they have been removed, so this flower has no pollen of its own. The bag also prevents pollen from any other flower from reaching the stigma. Without pollination, fertilisation cannot take place, so no seeds can be formed.
markPoints: No pollen available, because the anthers were removed and the bag blocks outside pollen
Without pollination there is no fertilisation, so no seeds form
questions.whyMarksLost: The bag matters. An answer that only mentions the removed anthers has not explained why pollen from elsewhere could not arrive.

questions.commandDemand: Give a similarity and a difference, referring to both processes in each point.
questions.stem: Compare pollination and fertilisation in a flowering plant.

fuzzyTraps.precise: fertilisation is the fusion of the male and female sex cells, which occurs after pollination

chain.text: Both are stages in sexual reproduction and both involve the pollen grain.
Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma.
Fertilisation is the fusion of the male sex cell with the female sex cell in the ovule.

questions.modelAnswer: Both pollination and fertilisation are stages in the sexual reproduction of a flowering plant, and both involve the pollen grain. However, pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma, while fertilisation is the fusion of the male sex cell from the pollen grain with the female sex cell inside the ovule. Pollination must happen before fertilisation can occur.
markPoints: Similarity: both are stages of sexual reproduction involving the pollen grain
Difference: pollination is transfer of pollen; fertilisation is the fusion of sex cells
questions.whyMarksLost: Students often define pollination twice. Fertilisation is a fusion, not a movement, and the word fusion is what earns the mark.

questions.commandDemand: Use the results to draw a conclusion, quoting which plants you are comparing.
questions.stimulus:
Four identical flowering plants were treated differently and the number of fruits produced was counted.

Plant 1, left uncovered outdoors: 24 fruits
Plant 2, covered with a fine mesh bag: 2 fruits
Plant 3, covered with a fine mesh bag, pollen brushed onto stigmas by hand: 21 fruits
Plant 4, anthers removed and left uncovered: 19 fruits
questions.stem: What can you infer from these results about how this plant is pollinated?

fuzzyTraps.precise: the mesh bag prevented insects from reaching the flowers, so pollination did not occur

chain.text: Plant 2, bagged, produced almost no fruit, so an outside agent is needed.
Plant 3, bagged but hand pollinated, produced nearly as much as Plant 1, so pollen transfer was the missing step.
Plant 4, with no anthers, still fruited, so the pollen came from another plant.

questions.modelAnswer: This plant relies on an outside agent, most likely insects, to carry pollen from another plant. Plant 2 was bagged and produced almost no fruit, showing that something was being blocked. Plant 3 was also bagged but had pollen brushed on by hand and produced 21 fruits, showing that the missing step was the transfer of pollen to the stigma. Plant 4 had its anthers removed yet still produced 19 fruits, showing that the pollen must have come from a different plant.
markPoints: An external agent, such as insects, transfers the pollen, supported by Plants 2 and 3
The pollen comes from another plant, supported by Plant 4
questions.whyMarksLost: Plant 4 is the one most students ignore, and it carries the second mark. When a table has four rows, every row is there for a reason.
